According to Mark Gurman's latest issue of the *Power On* newsletter, Apple is reportedly considering making changes to its App Store. The goal? To boost the potential revenue the platform brings in.

The details of Apple's plans for the App Store remain unclear. Bloomberg reporter Mark Gurman reports that Apple wants to 'find ways to increase profit margins and squeeze more recurring revenue out of the platform,' a work being primarily driven by new CEO John Ternus and current Services SVP Eddy Cue.

Reportedly, this effort was part of the reason longtime Apple executive Phil Schiller left the company last week. Schiller became an Apple Fellow after stepping down as SVP of Marketing in 2020, with part of his responsibilities including overseeing the App Store. Schiller was not on board with the concept:

There are many ways Apple could boost App Store profit margins. They could do away with their human app review process — in the era of agentic coding, this could be costly without delivering meaningful results. However, users may not appreciate further automated app review, even if it would help lower costs.

Apple could raise developer membership fees, currently $99 per year. Given that many small developers are already paying $200 a month for subscriptions to Codex and Claude to build apps, you could say Apple has room to raise prices and developers would still pay. Apple could also charge large developers subscription fees based on traffic, passing on some infrastructure costs.

What the result will be remains to be seen over time, but I for one am curious to see what these changes eventually look like.
